claim: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder whose neurodevelopmental symptoms include impaired executive function, attention, and spatial learning.
source: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder whose neurodevelopmental symptoms include impaired executive function, attention, and spatial learning and could be due to perturbed mesolimbic dopaminergic circuitry.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of NF1, drawing from established scientific knowledge about the disorder.

claim: NF1 mice exhibit reduced spontaneous dopaminergic neurotransmission.
source: We found that NF1 mice exhibit reduced spontaneous dopaminergic neurotransmission that was associated with excitation/inhibition imbalance in the ventral tegmental area and abnormal neuronal morphology.
evidence: This finding is presented in the abstract as a result from the study using dLight1.2 monitoring.

claim: Reduced spontaneous dopaminergic neurotransmission in NF1 mice is associated with excitation/inhibition imbalance in the ventral tegmental area.
source: We found that NF1 mice exhibit reduced spontaneous dopaminergic neurotransmission that was associated with excitation/inhibition imbalance in the ventral tegmental area and abnormal neuronal morphology.
evidence: This association is stated in the abstract based on experimental findings from patch clamp electrophysiology.

claim: NF1 mice exhibit abnormal neuronal morphology in dopaminergic neurons.
source: We found that NF1 mice exhibit reduced spontaneous dopaminergic neurotransmission that was associated with excitation/inhibition imbalance in the ventral tegmental area and abnormal neuronal morphology.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from morphological reconstruction studies.

claim: NF1 mice have more robust dopaminergic and behavioral responses to salient visual stimuli.
source: NF1 mice also had more robust dopaminergic and behavioral responses to salient visual stimuli, which were independent of learning, and rescued by optogenetic inhibition of non-dopaminergic neurons in the VTA.
evidence: This finding is presented in the abstract based on behavioral and photometry experiments.

claim: Enhanced dopaminergic and behavioral responses to salient visual stimuli in NF1 mice are independent of learning.
source: NF1 mice also had more robust dopaminergic and behavioral responses to salient visual stimuli, which were independent of learning, and rescued by optogenetic inhibition of non-dopaminergic neurons in the VTA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract based on experimental observations during conditioning tasks.

claim: Enhanced dopaminergic and behavioral responses to salient visual stimuli in NF1 mice are rescued by optogenetic inhibition of non-dopaminergic neurons in the VTA.
source: NF1 mice also had more robust dopaminergic and behavioral responses to salient visual stimuli, which were independent of learning, and rescued by optogenetic inhibition of non-dopaminergic neurons in the VTA.
evidence: This rescue effect is stated in the abstract based on optogenetic manipulation experiments.

claim: Neurofibromatosis type 1 affects approximately 1 in 3500 individuals worldwide.
source: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder of neural crest-derived tissues that affects approximately 1 in 3500 individuals worldwide and is caused by loss of one functional copy of the NF1 gene on chromosome 17 (Wallace et al., 1990).
evidence: This prevalence is stated in the introduction with a citation to Wallace et al., 1990.

claim: NF1 is caused by loss of one functional copy of the NF1 gene on chromosome 17.
source: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder of neural crest-derived tissues that affects approximately 1 in 3500 individuals worldwide and is caused by loss of one functional copy of the NF1 gene on chromosome 17 (Wallace et al., 1990).
evidence: This genetic cause is stated in the introduction with a citation to Wallace et al., 1990.

claim: Neurofibromin inhibits Ras-dependent cellular growth and proliferation.
source: Neurofibromin, the protein product of NF1, inhibits Ras-dependent cellular growth and proliferation (Basu et al., 1992) and enhances cAMP signaling pathways (Tong et al., 2002).
evidence: This function of neurofibromin is stated in the introduction with a citation to Basu et al., 1992.

claim: Neurofibromin enhances cAMP signaling pathways.
source: Neurofibromin, the protein product of NF1, inhibits Ras-dependent cellular growth and proliferation (Basu et al., 1992) and enhances cAMP signaling pathways (Tong et al., 2002).
evidence: This function of neurofibromin is stated in the introduction with a citation to Tong et al., 2002.

claim: Up to 70% of NF1-affected individuals experience impaired executive functioning, speech and language delays, attention deficits, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity.
source: Cognitive dysfunction is a significant source of lifetime morbidity, as up to 70% of affected individuals experience impaired executive functioning, speech and language delays, attention deficits, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity (Hyman et al., 2005).
evidence: This prevalence of cognitive symptoms is stated in the introduction with a citation to Hyman et al., 2005.

claim: Approximately one third of patients with NF1 meet DSM-V criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
source: Furthermore, approximately one third of patients with NF1 meet DSM-V criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (Hyman et al., 2005; Miguel et al., 2015).
evidence: This prevalence of ADHD in NF1 patients is stated in the introduction with citations to Hyman et al., 2005 and Miguel et al., 2015.

claim: Homozygous genetic disruption of the Nf1 gene is embryonic lethal in mice.
source: Although homozygous genetic disruption of the Nf1 gene is embryonic lethal in mice (Silva et al., 1997), cognitive deficits in NF1 have been successfully modeled in several transgenic and conditional knockout mouse lines (Silva et al., 1997; Zhu et al., 2001; Hegedus et al., 2007; Cui et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2010a; Anastasaki et al., 2015; Omrani et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2016).
evidence: This lethality is stated in the introduction with a citation to Silva et al., 1997.

claim: Heterozygous knockout mice (Nf1+/-) exhibit impaired spatial learning.
source: Heterozygous knockout mice (Nf1+/-) exhibit impaired spatial learning (Costa et al., 2001; Silva et al., 1997), which is Ras/ERK-dependent (Costa et al., 2002), rescued by the Ras inhibitor lovastatin (Li et al., 2005), and may be due to increased inhibitory GABA tone (Costa et al., 2002).
evidence: This behavioral phenotype is stated in the introduction with citations to Costa et al., 2001 and Silva et al., 1997.

claim: Impaired spatial learning in Nf1+/- mice is Ras/ERK-dependent.
source: Heterozygous knockout mice (Nf1+/-) exhibit impaired spatial learning (Costa et al., 2001; Silva et al., 1997), which is Ras/ERK-dependent (Costa et al., 2002), rescued by the Ras inhibitor lovastatin (Li et al., 2005), and may be due to increased inhibitory GABA tone (Costa et al., 2002).
evidence: This mechanistic finding is stated in the introduction with a citation to Costa et al., 2002.

claim: Impaired spatial learning in Nf1+/- mice is rescued by the Ras inhibitor lovastatin.
source: Heterozygous knockout mice (Nf1+/-) exhibit impaired spatial learning (Costa et al., 2001; Silva et al., 1997), which is Ras/ERK-dependent (Costa et al., 2002), rescued by the Ras inhibitor lovastatin (Li et al., 2005), and may be due to increased inhibitory GABA tone (Costa et al., 2002).
evidence: This rescue effect is stated in the introduction with a citation to Li et al., 2005.

claim: Impaired spatial learning in Nf1+/- mice may be due to increased inhibitory GABA tone.
source: Heterozygous knockout mice (Nf1+/-) exhibit impaired spatial learning (Costa et al., 2001; Silva et al., 1997), which is Ras/ERK-dependent (Costa et al., 2002), rescued by the Ras inhibitor lovastatin (Li et al., 2005), and may be due to increased inhibitory GABA tone (Costa et al., 2002).
evidence: This hypothesized mechanism is stated in the introduction with a citation to Costa et al., 2002.

claim: The neurofibromin C-terminus is a positive regulator of G-protein-stimulated adenylyl cyclase activity.
source: Additionally, the neurofibromin C-terminus is a positive regulator of G-protein-stimulated adenylyl cyclase activity (Hannan et al., 2006; Tong et al., 2002), and cAMP deficiency in NF1 knockout models causes altered in vitro neuronal morphology and growth, visual learning deficits, and changes in cortical architecture in mice (Brown et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2010b; Hegedus et al., 2007; Wolman et al., 2014).
evidence: This function is stated in the introduction with citations to Hannan et al., 2006 and Tong et al., 2002.

claim: cAMP deficiency in NF1 knockout models causes altered in vitro neuronal morphology and growth.
source: Additionally, the neurofibromin C-terminus is a positive regulator of G-protein-stimulated adenylyl cyclase activity (Hannan et al., 2006; Tong et al., 2002), and cAMP deficiency in NF1 knockout models causes altered in vitro neuronal morphology and growth, visual learning deficits, and changes in cortical architecture in mice (Brown et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2010b; Hegedus et al., 2007; Wolman et al., 2014).
evidence: This causal relationship is stated in the introduction with citations to Brown et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2010b; Hegedus et al., 2007; Wolman et al., 2014.

claim: cAMP deficiency in NF1 knockout models causes visual learning deficits.
source: Additionally, the neurofibromin C-terminus is a positive regulator of G-protein-stimulated adenylyl cyclase activity (Hannan et al., 2006; Tong et al., 2002), and cAMP deficiency in NF1 knockout models causes altered in vitro neuronal morphology and growth, visual learning deficits, and changes in cortical architecture in mice (Brown et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2010b; Hegedus et al., 2007; Wolman et al., 2014).
evidence: This causal relationship is stated in the introduction with citations to Brown et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2010b; Hegedus et al., 2007; Wolman et al., 2014.

claim: cAMP deficiency in NF1 knockout models causes changes in cortical architecture in mice.
source: Additionally, the neurofibromin C-terminus is a positive regulator of G-protein-stimulated adenylyl cyclase activity (Hannan et al., 2006; Tong et al., 2002), and cAMP deficiency in NF1 knockout models causes altered in vitro neuronal morphology and growth, visual learning deficits, and changes in cortical architecture in mice (Brown et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2010b; Hegedus et al., 2007; Wolman et al., 2014).
evidence: This causal relationship is stated in the introduction with citations to Brown et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2010b; Hegedus et al., 2007; Wolman et al., 2014.

claim: Mesolimbic reward circuits involve the convergence of dopaminergic projections from the midbrain ventral tegmental area (VTA) with glutamatergic inputs from cortical and subcortical regions on medium spiny neurons in the nucleus accumbens (NAc).
source: Mesolimbic reward circuits involve the convergence of dopaminergic projections from the midbrain ventral tegmental area (VTA) with glutamatergic inputs from cortical and subcortical regions on medium spiny neurons in the nucleus accumbens (NAc).
evidence: This anatomical description is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about mesolimbic circuits.

claim: Mesolimbic circuits facilitate the translation of relevant internal and external stimuli into motivated behaviors.
source: These circuits facilitate the translation of relevant internal and external stimuli into motivated behaviors (Wise, 2005) and have been implicated in the pathophysiology of ADHD and other disorders of impulse control (Li et al., 2006; Purper-Ouakil et al., 2011).
evidence: This functional role is stated in the introduction with a citation to Wise, 2005.

claim: Mesolimbic circuits have been implicated in the pathophysiology of ADHD and other disorders of impulse control.
source: These circuits facilitate the translation of relevant internal and external stimuli into motivated behaviors (Wise, 2005) and have been implicated in the pathophysiology of ADHD and other disorders of impulse control (Li et al., 2006; Purper-Ouakil et al., 2011).
evidence: This implication is stated in the introduction with citations to Li et al., 2006 and Purper-Ouakil et al., 2011.

claim: In the optic glioma mouse model of NF1, reduced striatal dopamine is associated with motor, exploratory, spatial learning, and attentional abnormalities.
source: In the optic glioma mouse model of NF1 (OPG, a conditional Nf1 knockout in astrocytes on an Nf1+/- background), reduced striatal dopamine is associated with motor, exploratory, spatial learning, and attentional abnormalities (Brown et al., 2010a; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013; Anastasaki et al., 2015), which are ameliorated by treatment with the catecholamine re-uptake inhibitor methylphenidate or the dopamine precursor L-DOPA (Brown et al., 2010a).
evidence: This association is stated in the introduction with citations to Brown et al., 2010a; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013; Anastasaki et al., 2015.

claim: Motor, exploratory, spatial learning, and attentional abnormalities in the optic glioma mouse model are ameliorated by treatment with methylphenidate or L-DOPA.
source: In the optic glioma mouse model of NF1 (OPG, a conditional Nf1 knockout in astrocytes on an Nf1+/- background), reduced striatal dopamine is associated with motor, exploratory, spatial learning, and attentional abnormalities (Brown et al., 2010a; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013; Anastasaki et al., 2015), which are ameliorated by treatment with the catecholamine re-uptake inhibitor methylphenidate or the dopamine precursor L-DOPA (Brown et al., 2010a).
evidence: This amelioration is stated in the introduction with a citation to Brown et al., 2010a.

claim: Dopaminergic neurotransmission has never been investigated in NF1 models in vivo.
source: Despite these efforts, dopaminergic neurotransmission has never been investigated in NF1 models in vivo.
evidence: This gap in knowledge is explicitly stated in the introduction.

claim: dLight1.2 allows for sub-micromolar detection of extracellular dopamine concentrations with sub-second resolution.
source: In order to investigate dopamine dynamics in freely behaving Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice, we utilized the genetically encoded, fluorescent dopamine sensor dLight1.2 (Patriarchi et al., 2018), which allows for sub-micromolar detection of extracellular dopamine concentrations with sub-second resolution and negligible sensitivity to other monoamines, GABA, and glutamate (Corre et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This technical capability is stated in the Results section with citations to Corre et al., 2018 and Patriarchi et al., 2018.

claim: dLight1.2 has negligible sensitivity to other monoamines, GABA, and glutamate.
source: In order to investigate dopamine dynamics in freely behaving Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice, we utilized the genetically encoded, fluorescent dopamine sensor dLight1.2 (Patriarchi et al., 2018), which allows for sub-micromolar detection of extracellular dopamine concentrations with sub-second resolution and negligible sensitivity to other monoamines, GABA, and glutamate (Corre et al., 2018; Patriarchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This specificity is stated in the Results section with citations to Corre et al., 2018 and Patriarchi et al., 2018.

claim: The dopamine transient event rate was reduced in Nf1+/- mice compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
source: Peak analysis was performed to identify local trace prominences (Figure 1D) and revealed that the dopamine transient event rate was reduced in Nf1+/- mice compared to Nf1+/+ littermates (Figure 1E).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Baseline (median) fluorescence, peak amplitude, and full width at half maximal intensity (FWHM) were equivalent between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes.
source: Baseline (median) fluorescence, peak amplitude, and full width at half maximal intensity (FWHM) was equivalent between genotypes.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section based on peak analysis of dLight1.2 signals.

claim: No differences in dopamine (DA), serotonin (5-HT), norepinephrine (NE), or their metabolites were detected between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes in the NAc.
source: We failed to detect differences in dopamine (DA), serotonin (5-HT), norepinephrine (NE), or their metabolites between genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no difference in dopaminergic terminal tyrosine hydroxylase expression across striatal sub-compartments between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice.
source: Additionally, there was no difference in dopaminergic terminal tyrosine hydroxylase expression across striatal sub-compartments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Basal differences in dLight1.2 event rate are not due to changes in dopaminergic terminal density or dopamine synthetic capacity.
source: These findings suggest that basal differences in dLight1.2 event rate are not due to changes in dopaminergic terminal density or dopamine synthetic capacity.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on HPLC and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Putative dopaminergic neurons in Nf1+/- midbrain slices exhibited lower spontaneous whole-cell firing rates compared to Nf1+/+ neurons.
source: We found that putative dopaminergic neurons in Nf1+/- midbrain slices exhibited lower spontaneous whole-cell firing rates (Figure 1G) and required more rheobase current to elicit a spike when compared to Nf1+/+ neurons (Figure 1H).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons required more rheobase current to elicit a spike compared to Nf1+/+ neurons.
source: We found that putative dopaminergic neurons in Nf1+/- midbrain slices exhibited lower spontaneous whole-cell firing rates (Figure 1G) and required more rheobase current to elicit a spike when compared to Nf1+/+ neurons (Figure 1H).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Phenotypic differences in baseline dLight1.2 event metrics are activity-dependent.
source: This finding supports the hypothesis that phenotypic differences in baseline dLight1.2 event metrics are activity-dependent.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on electrophysiology findings.

claim: Action potential threshold, duration, amplitude, and after hyperpolarization magnitude did not differ between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes.
source: Action potential threshold, duration, amplitude, and after hyperpolarization magnitude did not differ between genotypes (Figure 1I–J, Table 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1I-J and Table 1.

claim: Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons had increased input resistance (Rm) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
source: During whole-cell recordings, we also observed that Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons exhibit increased input resistance (Rm) and decreased membrane capacitance (Cm) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates (Figure 2A) without a change in other membrane properties (Table 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons had decreased membrane capacitance (Cm) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
source: During whole-cell recordings, we also observed that Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons exhibit increased input resistance (Rm) and decreased membrane capacitance (Cm) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates (Figure 2A) without a change in other membrane properties (Table 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cross-sectional area, major axis length, and minor axis length of VTA dopaminergic somata were reduced in Nf1+/- mice.
source: We found that cross-sectional area, major axis length, and minor axis length were reduced in Nf1+/- mice (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Soma aspect ratio was equivalent between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes.
source: Proportionality was maintained, however, as the soma aspect ratio was equivalent between genotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TH immunofluorescence and total neuron counts in the VTA did not differ between Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ dopaminergic neurons.
source: TH immunofluorescence and total neuron counts in the VTA did not differ between Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ dopaminergic neurons (Figure 2D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No phenotypic differences in soma size were observed in the adjacent substantia nigra pars compacta.
source: No phenotypic differences were observed in the adjacent substantia nigra pars compacta (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Relative differences in soma size were VTA-specific.
source: These findings indicate that relative differences in soma size were VTA-specific and could have contributed to changes in passive membrane properties.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on morphological analysis.

claim: No difference in dendritic complexity or total neurite length was observed between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes.
source: No difference in dendritic complexity or total neurite length was observed between genotypes (Figure 2H), which suggests that, although Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons have smaller somata than Nf1+/+ neurons, they have similar neurite morphology.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons had smaller Ih current amplitudes compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
source: We found that Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons had smaller Ih current amplitudes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) without a change in voltage dependence (Figure 3B; determined by tail current analysis) relative to Nf1+/+ littermates.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no change in Ih voltage dependence between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons.
source: We found that Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons had smaller Ih current amplitudes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) without a change in voltage dependence (Figure 3B; determined by tail current analysis) relative to Nf1+/+ littermates.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Differences in Ih current amplitudes were not significant when normalized to cell capacitance.
source: Differences in Ih current amplitudes were not significant when normalized to the cell capacitance to account for cell size (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and maximum Ih current amplitude was significantly correlated with Cm across all animals and within genotypes (Figure 3D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Maximum Ih current amplitude was significantly correlated with Cm across all animals and within genotypes.
source: Differences in Ih current amplitudes were not significant when normalized to the cell capacitance to account for cell size (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and maximum Ih current amplitude was significantly correlated with Cm across all animals and within genotypes (Figure 3D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Addition of 20 µM forskolin to the bath solution did not significantly affect Ih magnitude or voltage dependence in Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons.
source: Addition of 20 µM forskolin to the bath solution did not significantly affect Ih magnitude or voltage dependence in Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changes in Ih magnitude are likely cAMP-independent and reflective of smaller cell size.
source: Thus, changes in Ih magnitude are likely cAMP-independent, reflective of smaller cell size, and unlikely to be the etiologic cause of reduced cell excitability.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on forskolin experiments.

claim: Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons displayed increased sIPSC frequency compared to Nf1+/+ neurons.
source: We found that Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons displayed increased sIPSC frequency but not sIPSC amplitude, sEPSC frequency, or sEPSC amplitude compared to Nf1+/+ neurons (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: No differences in sIPSC amplitude, sEPSC frequency, or sEPSC amplitude were observed between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- neurons.
source: We found that Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons displayed increased sIPSC frequency but not sIPSC amplitude, sEPSC frequency, or sEPSC amplitude compared to Nf1+/+ neurons (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: Addition of 100 µM picrotoxin to the bath solution rescued spontaneous firing rates in Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons.
source: Addition of 100 µM picrotoxin (a highly selective, non-competitive GABAA receptor antagonist) to the bath solution rescued spontaneous firing rates in Nf1+/- putative dopaminergic neurons (Figure 3H) without affecting passive membrane properties (Table 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Picrotoxin reduced rheobase to levels significantly lower than control- and picrotoxin-treated Nf1+/+ cells.
source: Picrotoxin also reduced rheobase to levels significantly lower than control- and picrotoxin-treated Nf1+/+ cells (Figure 3I), which would be expected at baseline due to differences in soma volume.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Pre-treating Nf1+/- mice with morphine sulfate (5 mg/kg, s.c.) raised spontaneous dLight1.2 transient event rate.
source: We found that pre-treating Nf1+/- mice with the mu opioid receptor agonist morphine sulfate (5 mg/kg, s.c.) raised spontaneous dLight1.2 transient event rate but not event magnitude or FWHM relative to saline (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Morphine sulfate did not affect dLight1.2 event magnitude or FWHM in Nf1+/- mice.
source: We found that pre-treating Nf1+/- mice with the mu opioid receptor agonist morphine sulfate (5 mg/kg, s.c.) raised spontaneous dLight1.2 transient event rate but not event magnitude or FWHM relative to saline (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Excitation/inhibition imbalance is a mechanism gating Nf1+/- dopaminergic excitability ex vivo.
source: Thus, excitation/inhibition imbalance is a mechanism gating Nf1+/- dopaminergic excitability ex vivo, and attenuation of VTA GABAergic neurotransmission normalizes spontaneous LNAc dopaminergic neurotransmission in vivo.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on picrotoxin and morphine experiments.

claim: Attenuation of VTA GABAergic neurotransmission normalizes spontaneous LNAc dopaminergic neurotransmission in vivo.
source: Thus, excitation/inhibition imbalance is a mechanism gating Nf1+/- dopaminergic excitability ex vivo, and attenuation of VTA GABAergic neurotransmission normalizes spontaneous LNAc dopaminergic neurotransmission in vivo.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on morphine experiments.

claim: Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice observed robust LNAc dopamine transients time-locked to reward consumption that were not significantly different between genotypes.
source: In both Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ mice, we observed robust LNAc dopamine transients time-locked to reward consumption (Figure 4A) that were not significantly different between genotypes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: No difference in the number of rewards consumed during the 30 min session was observed between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- groups.
source: No difference in the number of rewards consumed during the 30 min session was observed between groups (Figure 4C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Large dopamine transients were observed at the onset of interaction with a novel, sex-matched, juvenile conspecific that was independent of genotype.
source: We observed large transients at the onset of interaction with a novel, sex-matched, juvenile conspecific that was independent of genotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ littermates failed to display differences in preference for a novel mouse in a social preference task.
source: Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ littermates also failed to display differences in preference for a novel mouse in a social preference task (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: LNAc dopamine and behavioral responses to unconditioned rewards are preserved in the context of Nf1 haploinsufficiency.
source: These findings suggest that LNAc dopamine and behavioral responses to unconditioned rewards are preserved in the context of Nf1 haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on reward consumption and social interaction experiments.

claim: No differences in the number of licks during the CS, the number of anticipatory licks, or the learning rate were observed between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice during Pavlovian conditioning.
source: No differences in the number of licks during the CS, the number of anticipatory licks, or the learning rate (the slope of the linear fit of CS licks across trials) were observed between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: dLight1.2 responses to the CS and US were enhanced and diminished, respectively, in mice that successfully learned the cue-reward association.
source: Similar to previous studies (Patriarchi et al., 2018), dLight1.2 responses to the CS and US (Figure 4G) were enhanced and diminished, respectively, in mice that successfully learned the cue-reward association (i.e. the learning rate was correlated with the rate of change of each feature peak across trials; (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section with a citation to Patriarchi et al., 2018 and supported by data shown in Figure 4G-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Unexpected omission of the US following CS presentation after learning equivalently diminished the dopamine response to reward seeking in both Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ mice.
source: Unexpected omission of the US following CS presentation after learning equivalently diminished the dopamine response to reward seeking in both Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ mice (Figure 4I), which is consistent with the role of dopamine in reward prediction error detection (Schultz et al., 2015).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section with a citation to Schultz et al., 2015 and supported by data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Nf1+/- mice displayed enhanced dLight1.2 responses to CS presentation on the first day of testing compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
source: Nf1+/- mice displayed enhanced dLight1.2 responses to CS presentation on the first day of testing (Figure 4J, inset) compared to Nf1+/+ littermates that was largest during the first trial (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The magnitude of the CS response on the first day of testing did not predict task performance in later sessions.
source: The magnitude of the CS response on the first day of testing did not predict task performance in later sessions (Session one vs Session 10; Nf1+/+: R2 = 0.02, p=0.69; Nf1+/-: R2 = 0.0006, p=0.94).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section based on correlation analysis.

claim: The ability to form cue-reward associations is equivalent between Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- genotypes.
source: These findings indicate that, although CS responses are larger in Nf1+/- mice, the ability to form cue-reward associations is equivalent between genotypes and coincides with adaptive changes in dopaminergic neurotransmission with learning.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on Pavlovian conditioning experiments.

claim: Both Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice exhibited trial-by-trial increases in freezing during the first seven trials of cued fear conditioning that subsequently plateaued.
source: Over the course of fifteen CS-US pairings, both Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice exhibited trial-by-trial increases in freezing during the first seven trials that subsequently plateaued (Figure 5A).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In both genotypes, the expression of freezing in later trials was correlated with the acquisition rate and the latency to freeze.
source: In both genotypes, the expression of freezing in later trials (average freezing time, trials 8–15) was correlated with the acquisition rate (slope of the linear fit, trials 1–7; Figure 5B) and the latency to freeze (trials 8–15; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The freezing acquisition rate and average freezing time was lower in Nf1+/- mice compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
source: Compared to Nf1+/+ littermates, both the acquisition rate and average freezing time was lower in Nf1+/- mice, which could be accounted for by an increased latency to freeze (Figure 5C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Nf1+/- mice had an increased latency to freeze during cued fear conditioning.
source: Compared to Nf1+/+ littermates, both the acquisition rate and average freezing time was lower in Nf1+/- mice, which could be accounted for by an increased latency to freeze (Figure 5C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Presentation of the CS resulted in several seconds of locomotor stimulation in Nf1+/- mice that delayed freezing.
source: Qualitative review of behavioral video recordings revealed that presentation of the CS resulted in several seconds of locomotor stimulation in Nf1+/- mice that delayed freezing (Video 1), whereas Nf1+/+ mice froze with short latency at CS onset once learning had occurred (Video 2).
evidence: This observation is stated in the Results section and supported by Video 1.

claim: A dopamine transient was observed at the onset of CS presentation that was greatest in trial 1, attenuated across trials, and was larger in Nf1+/- mice.
source: During LNAc dLight1.2 monitoring, a dopamine transient was observed at the onset of CS presentation that was greatest in trial 1, attenuated across trials, and was larger in Nf1+/- mice (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: In Nf1+/- but not Nf1+/+ mice, the magnitude of the CS peak during trial one was negatively correlated with acquisition rate and freezing duration and positively correlated with latency to freeze.
source: In Nf1+/- but not Nf1+/+ mice, the magnitude of the CS peak during trial one was negatively correlated with acquisition rate and freezing duration and positively correlated with latency to freeze (Figure 5F–G, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5F-G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Nf1+/- mice had significantly larger initial US peak responses compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
source: During US exposure, Nf1+/- mice had significantly larger initial US peak responses and a smaller integrated post-US rebound compared to Nf1+/+ littermates (area under the curve; Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nf1+/- mice had a smaller integrated post-US rebound compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
source: During US exposure, Nf1+/- mice had significantly larger initial US peak responses and a smaller integrated post-US rebound compared to Nf1+/+ littermates (area under the curve; Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Nf1+/+ mice, the magnitude of the US anti-peak during trial one was negatively correlated with freezing and positively correlated with latency to freeze.
source: In Nf1+/+ mice, the magnitude of the US anti-peak during trial one was negatively correlated with freezing and positively correlated with latency to freeze (Figure 5I–J, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5I-J and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The magnitude of the integrated post-US rebound was negatively correlated with the latency to freeze in Nf1+/- mice.
source: Additionally, the magnitude of the integrated post-US rebound was negatively correlated with the latency to freeze in Nf1+/- mice (Figure 5I–J, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5I-J and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Both genotypes exhibited robust dopamine transients at the onset of the overhead light stimulus that returned to baseline within 1–2 s and decremented across trials.
source: Both genotypes exhibited robust dopamine transients at the onset of the overhead light stimulus that returned to baseline within 1–2 s (Figure 6A) and decremented across trials (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 60 dB, 3 kHz auditory tone evoked dopamine transients at stimulus onset that were comparatively smaller than light responses and non-trial-dependent.
source: In both Nf1+/+ mice and Nf1+/- mice, 60 dB, 3 kHz auditory tone evoked dopamine transients at stimulus onset (Figure 6B) that were comparatively smaller than light responses (Figure 6C) and non-trial-dependent (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6B-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nf1+/- mice exhibited larger responses to light but not tone onset.
source: Nf1+/- mice exhibited larger responses to light but not tone onset (Figure 6C), which was confirmed when traces were analyzed as ΔF/F rather than z-score (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The development of cued freezing in Nf1+/- mice was equivalent to Nf1+/+ littermates across the first ten trials when a tone-only CS was used.
source: We found that the development of cued freezing in Nf1+/- mice was equivalent to Nf1+/+ littermates across the first ten trials (Figure 6D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Addition of the overhead light stimulus to the CS was sufficient to perturb the expression of freezing in Nf1+/- but not Nf1+/+ mice by increasing the latency to freeze.
source: Addition of the overhead light stimulus to the CS was sufficient to perturb the expression of freezing in Nf1+/- but not Nf1+/+ mice by increasing the latency to freeze (Figure 6E, Video 3).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Video 3.

claim: Deficits in cued fear conditioning in Nf1+/- mice are reversible, visual stimulus-dependent, and independent of learning.
source: Thus, deficits in cued fear conditioning in Nf1+/- mice are reversible, visual stimulus-dependent, and independent of learning.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on tone-only fear conditioning experiments.

claim: Nf1+/+ and Nf1+/- mice had similar reaction times to a looming stimulus.
source: In response to the onset of the looming stimulus, both genotypes exhibited similar sub-second reaction times (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nf1+/- mice were more likely to escape to the shelter at looming stimulus onset compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
source: Compared to Nf1+/+ littermates, Nf1+/- mice were more likely to escape to the shelter at stimulus onset and exhibited shorter latencies to the first freezing episode (Figure 6F).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Nf1+/- mice exhibited shorter latencies to the first freezing episode during looming stimulus presentation compared to Nf1+/+ littermates.
source: Compared to Nf1+/+ littermates, Nf1+/- mice were more likely to escape to the shelter at stimulus onset and exhibited shorter latencies to the first freezing episode (Figure 6F).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Two seconds of vSC optogenetic stimulation produced time-locked, short latency dopamine release in the LNAc at stimulus onset that subsequently decayed to baseline.
source: Similar to overhead light exposure, two seconds of vSC optogenetic stimulation (5 mW, 20 Hz, 5 ms pulse width) produced time-locked, short latency dopamine release in the LNAc at stimulus onset that subsequently decayed to baseline (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: vSC ChR2 activation evoked vigorous escape behavior in the absence of a threatening stimulus.
source: During testing, we also observed that vSC ChR2 activation evoked vigorous escape behavior in the absence of a threatening stimulus (Video 4), as has been observed following photostimulation of vSC-to-VTA projections (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This observation is stated in the Results section with a citation to Zhou et al., 2019 and supported by Video 4.

claim: The SC can induce rapid dopamine release in the LNAc that is qualitatively similar to overhead light exposure.
source: These findings indicate that the SC, a visually responsive region involved in innate responses to salient visual stimuli (Ito and Feldheim, 2018), can induce rapid dopamine release in the LNAc that is qualitatively similar to overhead light exposure.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section with a citation to Ito and Feldheim, 2018 based on optogenetic experiments.

claim: Only 14.7% of NpHR-positive cells in the VTA expressed tyrosine hydroxylase.
source: Post hoc analysis revealed that only 14.7 ± 0.01% of NpHR-positive cells in the VTA expressed tyrosine hydroxylase (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 3), indicating successful targeting of VTAnon-Th neurons in Nf1+/- and Nf1+/+ mice.
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the absence of optogenetic inhibition, VTATh-Off-NpHR-eYFP Nf1+/- mice were more likely to escape to the shelter and exhibited shorter latency to the first freezing episode compared to VTATh-Off-mCherry Nf1+/+ mice.
source: In the absence of optogenetic inhibition, optical patch cable-tethered VTATh-Off-NpHR-eYFP Nf1+/- mice were more likely to escape to the available shelter in response to looming stimulus presentation and exhibited shorter latency to the first freezing episode when compared to VTATh-Off-mCherry Nf1+/+ mice (Figure 6I).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Delivery of 532 nm light to the VTA during looming stimulus presentation decreased the percentage of VTATh-Off-NpHR-eYFP Nf1+/- mice that escaped to the shelter to a level similar to Nf1+/+ mice.
source: Delivery of 532 nm light (5 mW, 30 Hz, 20 ms pulse width) to the VTA during looming stimulus presentation had no effect on VTATh-Off-mCherry Nf1+/+ mice but decreased the percentage of VTATh-Off-NpHR-eYFP Nf1+/- mice that escaped to the shelter to a level (33%) that was similar to Nf1+/+ mice (41%) and VTATh-Off-mCherry Nf1+/+ mice (42%) (Figure 6F–I; Video 5).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6F-I and Video 5.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of VTAnon-Th neurons increased the latency to the first freezing episode in VTATh-Off-NpHR-eYFP Nf1+/- mice to a level not significantly different from VTATh-Off-mCherry Nf1+/+ mice.
source: This shift in escape location coincided with an increase in the latency to the first freezing episode in VTATh-Off-NpHR-eYFP Nf1+/- mice that was not significantly different from VTATh-Off-mCherry Nf1+/+ mice (Figure 6I).
evidence: This finding is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of VTAnon-Th neurons normalizes looming stimulus responses in Nf1+/- mice.
source: Thus, optogenetic inhibition of VTAnon-Th neurons normalizes looming stimulus responses in Nf1+/- mice and supports a role for VTA GABAergic neurons in the expression of visual stimulus response phenotypes caused by Nf1 haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: VTA GABAergic neurons play a role in the expression of visual stimulus response phenotypes caused by Nf1 haploinsufficiency.
source: Thus, optogenetic inhibition of VTAnon-Th neurons normalizes looming stimulus responses in Nf1+/- mice and supports a role for VTA GABAergic neurons in the expression of visual stimulus response phenotypes caused by Nf1 haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section based on optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Increased tonic inhibition of Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons reduces basal activity.
source: Given these findings, it is likely that increased tonic inhibition of Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons reduces basal activity, whereas smaller soma volume acts as a compensatory mechanism to increase excitability during disinhibition.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Discussion based on experimental findings.

claim: Smaller soma volume acts as a compensatory mechanism to increase excitability during disinhibition in Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons.
source: Given these findings, it is likely that increased tonic inhibition of Nf1+/- dopaminergic neurons reduces basal activity, whereas smaller soma volume acts as a compensatory mechanism to increase excitability during disinhibition.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Discussion based on experimental findings.

claim: Excitation/inhibition imbalance is present in the amygdala, striatum, and medial prefrontal cortex of Nf1+/- mice.
source: Excitation/inhibition imbalance is present in the amygdala (Molosh et al., 2014; Repunte-Canonigo et al., 2015), striatum (Shilyansky et al., 2010), and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Gonçalves et al., 2017; Shilyansky et al., 2010) of Nf1+/- mice and likely contributes to deficits in working memory, contextual fear conditioning, and social memory (Cui et al., 2008; Molosh et al., 2014; Shilyansky et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Molosh et al., 2014; Repunte-Canonigo et al., 2015; Shilyansky et al., 2010; Gonçalves et al., 2017.

claim: Excitation/inhibition imbalance likely contributes to deficits in working memory, contextual fear conditioning, and social memory in Nf1+/- mice.
source: Excitation/inhibition imbalance is present in the amygdala (Molosh et al., 2014; Repunte-Canonigo et al., 2015), striatum (Shilyansky et al., 2010), and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Gonçalves et al., 2017; Shilyansky et al., 2010) of Nf1+/- mice and likely contributes to deficits in working memory, contextual fear conditioning, and social memory (Cui et al., 2008; Molosh et al., 2014; Shilyansky et al., 2010).
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Discussion with citations to Cui et al., 2008; Molosh et al., 2014; Shilyansky et al., 2010.

claim: Subthreshold doses of picrotoxin (0.01 mg/kg) improve cognitive performance of NF1 model mice.
source: Subthreshold doses of picrotoxin (0.01 mg/kg) (Cui et al., 2008) or L-DOPA (Wozniak et al., 2013) improve cognitive performance of NF1 model mice, emphasizing the therapeutic potential of interventions that modulate mesolimbic dopaminergic circuit function.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Cui et al., 2008.

claim: L-DOPA improves cognitive performance of NF1 model mice.
source: Subthreshold doses of picrotoxin (0.01 mg/kg) (Cui et al., 2008) or L-DOPA (Wozniak et al., 2013) improve cognitive performance of NF1 model mice, emphasizing the therapeutic potential of interventions that modulate mesolimbic dopaminergic circuit function.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Wozniak et al., 2013.

claim: The optic glioma (OPG) mouse model of NF1 has reduced tyrosine hydroxylase expression in the VTA.
source: This is in contrast with the optic glioma (OPG) mouse model of NF1 that has reduced tyrosine hydroxylase expression in the VTA (Brown et al., 2012; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013) and lower TH, dopamine, and phosphorylated DARPP-32 (dopamine and cAMP-regulated phosphoprotein-32) in terminal fields (Brown et al., 2010a; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013; Anastasaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Brown et al., 2012 and Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013.

claim: The optic glioma (OPG) mouse model of NF1 has lower TH, dopamine, and phosphorylated DARPP-32 in terminal fields.
source: This is in contrast with the optic glioma (OPG) mouse model of NF1 that has reduced tyrosine hydroxylase expression in the VTA (Brown et al., 2012; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013) and lower TH, dopamine, and phosphorylated DARPP-32 (dopamine and cAMP-regulated phosphoprotein-32) in terminal fields (Brown et al., 2010a; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013; Anastasaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Brown et al., 2010a; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013; Anastasaki et al., 2015.

claim: Neurite outgrowth and growth cone areas are decreased in cultured OPG dopaminergic neurons.
source: Neurite outgrowth and growth cone areas are decreased in cultured OPG dopaminergic neurons (Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013), yet we did not observe changes in neurite morphology in Th-VAST-labeled Nf1+/- neurons relative to Nf1+/+ littermates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013.

claim: Nf1+/- mice on a pure C57Bl/6 background have higher tissue neurofibromin levels compared to OPG mice.
source: Nf1+/- mice on a pure C57Bl/6 background have higher tissue neurofibromin levels compared to OPG mice, and neurofibromin dose-dependently regulates TH and cellular dopamine production in cultured mouse neurons and neural progenitor cells differentiated from patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (Anastasaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Anastasaki et al., 2015.

claim: Neurofibromin dose-dependently regulates TH and cellular dopamine production in cultured mouse neurons and neural progenitor cells differentiated from patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: Nf1+/- mice on a pure C57Bl/6 background have higher tissue neurofibromin levels compared to OPG mice, and neurofibromin dose-dependently regulates TH and cellular dopamine production in cultured mouse neurons and neural progenitor cells differentiated from patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (Anastasaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Anastasaki et al., 2015.

claim: cAMP deficiency influences the morphology of Nf1+/- and OPG neurons in vitro.
source: While the etiology of reduced soma volumes is unknown, cAMP deficiency influences the morphology of Nf1+/- and OPG neurons in vitro (Brown et al., 2012; Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Brown et al., 2012 and Diggs-Andrews et al., 2013.

claim: Adult and adolescent human subjects with NF1 exhibit visual processing deficits.
source: Adult and adolescent human subjects with NF1 exhibit visual processing deficits (Hyman et al., 2005), although visual cortical areas have sparse, if any, direct connections to VTA dopaminergic neurons (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Hyman et al., 2005.

claim: Visual cortical areas have sparse, if any, direct connections to VTA dopaminergic neurons.
source: Adult and adolescent human subjects with NF1 exhibit visual processing deficits (Hyman et al., 2005), although visual cortical areas have sparse, if any, direct connections to VTA dopaminergic neurons (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012.

claim: The superior colliculus receives direct input from retinal ganglion cells.
source: Short latency dopaminergic responses to visual stimuli are likely driven by afferents from the superior colliculus (SC) (Redgrave et al., 2010), which receives direct input from retinal ganglion cells (Dhande and Huberman, 2014), responds to looming stimuli (Zhao et al., 2014), and evokes firing of both VTA GABAergic and dopaminergic neurons in vivo while enhancing flight-to-shelter responses (Prévost-Solié et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Dhande and Huberman, 2014.

claim: The superior colliculus responds to looming stimuli.
source: Short latency dopaminergic responses to visual stimuli are likely driven by afferents from the superior colliculus (SC) (Redgrave et al., 2010), which receives direct input from retinal ganglion cells (Dhande and Huberman, 2014), responds to looming stimuli (Zhao et al., 2014), and evokes firing of both VTA GABAergic and dopaminergic neurons in vivo while enhancing flight-to-shelter responses (Prévost-Solié et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Zhao et al., 2014.

claim: The superior colliculus evokes firing of both VTA GABAergic and dopaminergic neurons in vivo while enhancing flight-to-shelter responses.
source: Short latency dopaminergic responses to visual stimuli are likely driven by afferents from the superior colliculus (SC) (Redgrave et al., 2010), which receives direct input from retinal ganglion cells (Dhande and Huberman, 2014), responds to looming stimuli (Zhao et al., 2014), and evokes firing of both VTA GABAergic and dopaminergic neurons in vivo while enhancing flight-to-shelter responses (Prévost-Solié et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Prévost-Solié et al., 2019 and Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: Flight-to-shelter responses to looming stimuli are mediated by VTA GABA neurons.
source: While the initial dopaminergic peak may serve as a salience signal, flight-to-shelter responses appear to be mediated by VTA GABA neurons (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Zhou et al., 2019.
